The drug should be stopped and he needs urgent same-day assessment.
why_wrong: A. Drug hepatitis can cause jaundice, but the known enzyme defect and oxidant drug make haemolysis far more likely. B. Nephrotic syndrome causes frothy urine and oedema, not jaundice. D. B12 deficiency develops slowly and would not follow a short course of an antibiotic. E. Marrow failure causes cytopenias, not acute jaundice and dark urine.
pearl: Heinz bodies and bite cells on the blood film are characteristic of oxidative haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
thinking: Known red cell enzyme defect ↓ New oxidant drug ↓ Dark urine and jaundice within days ↓ Oxidative damage to red cells ↓ Acute haemolysis
exam_trap: A, Drug-induced acute hepatitis — a new drug with jaundice suggests liver injury, but cola-coloured urine plus G6PD deficiency points to intravascular haemolysis.
takeaway: Oxidant drugs can cause acute haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

stem:
A 20-year-old university athlete is referred after a sports physician notes a palpable spleen. She recalls being yellow on and off since childhood, often during colds, and her father and grandmother both had their gallbladders removed young. Her blood film shows small dense red cells without central pallor.

Which inherited disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant, so it often shows a pattern across generations. Defects in red cell membrane proteins make cells spherical and rigid, so the spleen removes them early, giving episodic jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones. Spherocytes on the film fit this diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Thalassaemia trait causes a mild microcytic picture and is not typically associated with recurrent jaundice and splenomegaly. C. Carriers are usually well, without chronic haemolysis. D. Haemophilia is an X-linked clotting factor deficiency causing bleeding, not haemolysis. E. This causes mucosal bleeding, not jaundice or splenomegaly.
pearl: Splenectomy greatly reduces haemolysis in severe hereditary spherocytosis but is usually deferred until after early childhood because of infection risk.
thinking: Recurrent jaundice with infections ↓ Splenomegaly ↓ Family history of early gallstones ↓ Spherocytes on film ↓ Hereditary spherocytosis
exam_trap: A, Beta-thalassaemia trait — it is a common inherited red cell disorder, but carriers have a mild microcytosis and rarely have jaundice or a big spleen.
takeaway: Episodic jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes and an affected parent suggest hereditary spherocytosis.

stem:
On the haematology ward, a 52-year-old man with warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia has developed yellow sclerae. His urine is negative for bilirubin on dipstick testing, and his liver enzymes are normal.

Which type of bilirubin will make up most of the rise?

options.E: No rise; the yellow colour is due to carotenaemia

why_correct: Haemolysis increases haem breakdown, producing more bilirubin than the liver can conjugate, so the excess is mainly unconjugated. Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and not water-soluble, so it does not appear in the urine, which is why haemolytic jaundice is called acholuric. Normal liver enzymes support a pre-hepatic cause.
why_wrong: A. A conjugated rise suggests hepatocellular disease or biliary obstruction. B. Direct bilirubin is essentially conjugated bilirubin, which is not the main fraction in haemolysis. D. Bile acids rise in cholestasis, not haemolysis. E. Carotenaemia spares the sclerae, whereas his sclerae are yellow.
pearl: Gilbert's syndrome also gives an isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, but with no signs of haemolysis.
thinking: Known haemolytic anaemia ↓ Yellow sclerae ↓ No bilirubin in urine and normal liver enzymes ↓ Pre-hepatic cause ↓ Mainly unconjugated bilirubin
exam_trap: A, Conjugated bilirubin — jaundice is often linked with liver disease, but conjugated bilirubin would also appear in the urine, which it does not here.
takeaway: Haemolysis causes a mainly unconjugated (acholuric) hyperbilirubinaemia.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy, whose mother has hereditary spherocytosis, is reviewed in the paediatric clinic. He is pale, mildly jaundiced and has a palpable spleen tip. His blood film shows spherocytes and polychromasia, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.

How is his anaemia best classified?
why_correct: In hereditary spherocytosis, abnormal membrane proteins make red cells spherical and fragile, and they are removed early by the spleen. This shortened red cell survival is a haemolytic anaemia, shown here by jaundice, splenomegaly and polychromasia from increased reticulocytes. A negative direct antiglobulin test helps separate it from autoimmune haemolysis.
why_wrong: A. Megaloblastic anaemia results from B12 or folate deficiency and causes macrocytes, not spherocytes. B. Aplastic anaemia is marrow failure with pancytopenia and low reticulocytes. D. Iron deficiency causes small pale cells and no jaundice. E. There is no history of bleeding, and blood loss does not cause jaundice.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 can cause an aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis, with a sudden fall in haemoglobin and very low reticulocytes.
thinking: Affected parent ↓ Pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly ↓ Spherocytes and polychromasia ↓ Shortened red cell survival ↓ Haemolytic anaemia
exam_trap: B, Aplastic anaemia — aplastic crises do occur in this condition, but polychromasia shows an active marrow, which is the opposite of aplasia.
takeaway: Hereditary spherocytosis causes an extravascular haemolytic anaemia.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman who had two units of red cells after a hip replacement a week ago returns to the orthopaedic ward from home. She reports tea-coloured urine, and the nurse notes that her eyes look yellow. Her haemoglobin is lower than it was after the transfusion.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction usually occurs days to two weeks after transfusion, when previously formed red cell antibodies are boosted and destroy the transfused cells. Falling haemoglobin, jaundice and dark urine are typical. A direct antiglobulin test, haemolysis screen and repeat antibody screen are needed, and the transfusion laboratory should be told.
why_wrong: A. This causes breathlessness and pulmonary oedema during or soon after transfusion. C. This causes fever and rigors during or shortly after transfusion, without haemolysis. D. This causes acute respiratory distress within about six hours of transfusion. E. This is very rare in the UK and would not appear within a week or cause a falling haemoglobin.
pearl: Delayed haemolytic reactions are most likely in people previously sensitised by pregnancy or earlier transfusion; the antibody involved should be recorded to guide future transfusions.
thinking: Recent red cell transfusion ↓ A week later ↓ Jaundice and dark urine ↓ Haemoglobin falling ↓ Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction
exam_trap: E, Transfusion-transmitted viral hepatitis — jaundice after a blood product suggests infection, but the timing is too short and the falling haemoglobin points to haemolysis.
takeaway: Jaundice, dark urine and a falling haemoglobin days after transfusion suggest a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction.

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the ED by his grandmother two days after a family meal that included broad beans. He is pale and lethargic, with yellow eyes and dark urine. His haemoglobin has dropped, and the film shows bite cells.

Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: Broad (fava) beans contain oxidant compounds that can trigger acute haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, an X-linked enzyme defect that is more common in boys. Bite cells and Heinz bodies reflect oxidative damage to haemoglobin. Confirmation is by measuring G6PD activity.
why_wrong: A. This causes chronic haemolysis with spherocytes rather than a sudden episode after eating beans. B. This causes mild microcytosis without acute haemolytic episodes. C. This is a clotting disorder causing bleeding, not haemolysis. D. This causes mucosal bleeding, not jaundice and dark urine.
pearl: G6PD activity measured during or just after an acute haemolytic episode can be falsely normal, because young red cells have more enzyme, so testing is repeated a few months later if needed.
thinking: Boy, acute illness after broad beans ↓ Jaundice and dark urine ↓ Falling haemoglobin ↓ Bite cells show oxidative damage ↓ G6PD deficiency
exam_trap: A, Hereditary spherocytosis — it is the commonest inherited haemolytic anaemia in northern Europeans, but it does not produce food-triggered oxidative haemolysis or bite cells.
takeaway: Haemolysis after broad beans in a boy suggests G6PD deficiency.

presentation: Sickle cell disease presenting with painful crises
stem:
A 26-year-old woman who recently moved to the UK from Ghana registers with a GP. Since childhood she has had episodes of severe pain in her bones and joints, often after colds or cold weather, needing hospital care. Her bloods show a chronic anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count and bilirubin. Her brother had a stroke as a child.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder in which HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, causing rigid red cells that block small vessels and are destroyed early. This explains recurrent painful vaso-occlusive crises, triggered by infection, cold and dehydration, alongside chronic haemolysis. Childhood stroke in a sibling is another recognised complication. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. This causes a low platelet count with bruising and bleeding, not painful crises or haemolysis. B. This causes pancytopenia with low reticulocytes. D. This causes microcytosis without haemolysis or bone pain episodes. E. This causes macrocytic anaemia and neurological features, not recurrent bone pain crises.
pearl: Hydroxycarbamide raises fetal haemoglobin and reduces the frequency of painful crises in sickle cell disease.
thinking: West African heritage ↓ Lifelong recurrent bone and joint pain episodes ↓ Triggered by cold and infection ↓ Chronic haemolysis with reticulocytosis ↓ Sickle cell disease
exam_trap: D, Iron deficiency anaemia — anaemia is common in young women, but iron deficiency does not cause haemolysis or recurrent pain crises.
takeaway: Recurrent pain crises plus chronic haemolytic anaemia suggest sickle cell disease.
